questions.html:
Consider the following boolean equations:

  1. $b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c=b d+a c d^{\prime}$
  2. $(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(a+b+c)=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)$

Which of the above is correct?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 7)

Let $P = bd + acd' + abc $ and $Q = bd + acd'$, then

$\begin{align*}
bd + acd' + abc &= bd + acd' \qquad \text{(From Consensus property)} \\
P &= Q \qquad \\
\text{So,}\bf \text{ Eq. A is True.}
\end{align*}
$

Now,

$P^d = (bd + acd' + abc)^d = (b+d)(a+c+d')(a+b+c)$ and

$Q^d = (bd + acd')^d = (b+d)(a+c+d') $

$\text{If $\underbrace{P = Q}_{Eq.\ A}$ then $\underbrace{P^d = Q^d}_{Eq.\ B}$  $\qquad$ (From Principle of Duality)}$

$\text{So,}\bf \text{ Eq. B is True.}$

$\bf \therefore \text{Ans: C}$

Source solution 2 (score: 4)

$\text{Method 1(Direct):}$
Both are consensus theorems.

$\text{Method 2(Most Efficient):}$
Use the “By-Case” method that we have studied in lectures, as it is Most Efficient method.

$\text{Method 3 (Less Efficient):}$
The following method uses Boolean Algebra rules, but it is a VERY inefficient method compared to the “By-Case” method that we have studied in the lectures.

A. $b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c=b d+a c d^{\prime}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.S. } &=b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c & & \\
&=b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c .1 & & \text { (identity) } \\
&=b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c\left(d+d^{\prime}\right) & & \text { (complements) } \\
&=b d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c d+a b c d^{\prime} & & \text { (distributive) } \\
&=b d+a b c d+a c d^{\prime}+a b c d^{\prime} & & \text { (commutative) } \\
&=b d(1+a c)+a c d^{\prime}(1+b) & & \text { (distributive) } \\
&=b d+a c d^{\prime} & & \\
\text { L.H.S. } &=\text { R.H.S } &
\end{aligned}
$$
B. $(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(a+b+c)=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { L.H.S. } &=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(a+b+c) & & \\
&=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(a+b+c+0) & & \text { (identity) } \\
&=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)\left(a+b+c+d . d^{\prime}\right) & & \text { (complements) } \\
&=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(a+b+c+d)\left(a+b+c+d^{\prime}\right) & & \text { (distributive) } \\
&=(b+d)(a+b+c+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)\left(a+b+c+d^{\prime}\right) & & \text { (commutative) } \\
&=(b+d)(1+a+c)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right)(1+b) & & \text { (distributive) } \\
&=(b+d)\left(a+c+d^{\prime}\right) & & \\
\text { L.H.S. } &=\text { R.H.S } &
\end{aligned}
$$
Write your answer Or comment using the "By-Case" method.

For example when $(a, b, c, d)=(0,1,1,1)$, we have output $(\mathrm{S}_2, \mathrm{S}_1, \mathrm{S}_0)=(0,1,1)$, and when $(a,b,c,d)=(1,0,1,0)$, we have output $( \mathrm{S}_2, \mathrm{S}_1, \mathrm{S}_0)=(0,1,0)$.

Number of Prime Implicants of $\mathrm{S}_2?$

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

When $abcd = 1111$, then $(\mathrm{S}_2, \mathrm{~S}_1, \mathrm{~S} 0)=(1,0,0)$.

$\mathrm{S}_2$ is $1$ iff $abcd =1111$.

So, $\mathrm{S}_2 = abcd,$ Hence, one Prime Implicants which is $abcd$ itself.

Note that $\mathrm{S}_1$ is $1$ when the number of $1's$ in $abcd$ is either $2$ or $3.$

Hence, $\text{S}_1(a,b,c,d)$ will have the following MinTerms $=
3,5,6,7,9,10,11,12,13,14.$

questions.html:
A bit counting machine reads a binary input vector $(a, b, c, d)$ and produces a binary number $(\text{S}_{2},\text{S}_{1},\text{S}_{0})$ that counts the number of $1’\text{s}$ in the input bits. For example when $(a, b, c, d)=(0,1,1,1)$, we have output $(\text{S}_{2},\text{S}_{1},\text{S}_{0})=(0,1,1)$, and when $(a, b, c, d)=(1,0,1,0)$, we have output $(\text{S}_{2},\text{S}_{1},\text{S}_{0})=(0,1,0)$.

Let $\mathrm{Y(a,b,c,d)}$ be a boolean function such that $Y$ is $1$ for any input combination $(a,b,c,d)$ if and only if both $S_1,S_0$ are both $1$ for that input combination.

The number of Prime Implicants in $\text{Y}?$
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 7)

$\mathrm{Y(a,b,c,d)}=\mathrm{S}_1 \cdot \mathrm{S}_0$ is $1$ iff $\mathrm{S}_1=\mathrm{S}_0=1$ together.

It is possible only when $(\mathrm{S}_2, \mathrm{~S}_1, \mathrm{~S}_0)=(0,1,1)$ i.e. number of $1's$ in $abcd$ is $3.$

NOTE that $(\mathrm{S}_2, \mathrm{~S}_1, \mathrm{~S}_0)=(1,1,1)$ is NEVER possible because that would mean that we have $7$ one's in the input combination $(a,b,c,d)$.

So, for $\mathrm{Y}(a,b,c,d)$, True Minterms are $7,11,13,14.$

Hence, $4$ Prime Implicants.
